The **pistol** is the player 's default weapon, and fires bullets . Each player enters the game with a pistol, fifty bullets, and their fists , with the pistol selected as the active weapon. None of the monsters carry a pistol, though the trooper appears to be armed with a rifle that fires pistol bullets.

_"Pistol is your standard military-issued weapon.
It will stay with you, so don't forget about it if things get rough."_

― Doom instruction manual

## Combat characteristics [ [edit](https://doomwiki.org/w/index.php?title=Pistol&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Combat characteristics") ]

The pistol from Doom 64 , at the start of MAP01: Staging Area") .

The pistol fires individual bullets, each inflicting 5–15 points of damage . If the player holds the fire button down, the marine fires the pistol repeatedly. As with the chaingun , the initial shot accurately strikes the object in the centre of the screen, but if the trigger is held down, subsequent shots have a dispersal (standard deviation around 2°, to a maximum of ±5.5°).

## Tactical analysis [ [edit](https://doomwiki.org/w/index.php?title=Pistol&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Tactical analysis") ]
The pistol is a weak weapon, doing damage at a rate barely 10% greater than the fists and generally should not be used if any better weapon is available. However, if the player is low on shotgun shells and does not have the chaingun in their possession, the pistol can be used to take down individual or small groups of zombies or imps and save shells for pinkies or stronger enemies that may be encountered later. Owing to its perfect accuracy when fired once, the pistol is also a dependable weapon for killing low-tier monsters over long distances prior to finding the chaingun. This situation is most commonly suffered at the first levels of an episode or megawad especially on Ultra-Violence difficulty when the player is looking desperately for a shotgun, but still has to face great quantities of monsters.

The pistol is capable of 100% accurate fire if the player carefully taps the fire button slightly after the first shot rather than holding it down.
It is also the most economical way to shoot hitscan-activated switches, because unlike the chaingun, the pistol only fires one bullet per cycle rather than two (however when playing the original executable, the player may have to use the super shotgun as it is the only weapon with vertical spread to hit switches that may be on a higher level than the one the player is currently on).

## Notes [ [edit](https://doomwiki.org/w/index.php?title=Pistol&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Notes") ]

The pistol off-hand sprite can be seen in the HUD for the Super Nintendo") version when the weapon is selected.

* Because neither players nor monsters can drop a pistol, it is the only weapon (apart from the fists) that does not have a "pickup" sprite . An icon for the pistol can be seen in the Doom Collector's Edition and Final Doom instruction manuals, but this graphic does not appear in the game.

Assets released by John Romero also show an off-hand sprite for the pistol.
* The Doom 64 pistol has a new look. The gun is narrower, and looks more like a [Desert Eagle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Desert_Eagle "wikipedia:Desert Eagle") .

The **shotgun** (aka **Pump Shotgun** [[ 1 ]]() ) is one of the most versatile and useful weapons in the _Doom_ player 's arsenal, equipped in all classic _Doom_ games. It's a [pump-action shotgun](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Slide-action_shotgun "wikipedia:Slide-action shotgun") with a wooden stock. It has an old-fashioned look and is first found in a secret area of E1M1: Hangar (or possibly taken from a Shotgun Guy on the upper two skill levels ), then in a non-secret area on E1M2: Nuclear Plant .

A shotgun contains 8 shells when picked up (16 shells on the "I'm too young to die" and "Nightmare!" skill levels ).
Shotguns looted from the corpses of shotgun wielding zombies contain 4 shells (8 on ITYTD and NM) and, unlike pre-existing shotguns, disappear when crushed beneath doors or moving ceilings .

The player's shotgun fires seven pellets, each of which inflicts 5-15 points of damage (for a total of 35-105 points of damage per shot, provided that all pellets connect against the target). Each pellet has the same random directional offset as a pistol shot, which gives an aggregate horizontal spread between 2.2° and 9.8° (the average is 5.9°, and the standard deviation 1.5°). Unlike the super shotgun of _Doom II_ , which spreads pellets in a rough cone, there is no vertical dispersal; presumably this was a consequence of the game engine's predominantly planar design.

[The shotgun being used on](https://static.wikia.nocookie.net/doom/images/a/a4/MAP11_shotgun.png/revision/latest?cb=20090622034338) 

The shotgun being used on Level 11: 'O' of Destruction!")
The shotgun packs a deadly punch at close range, and the grouping of the pellets is tight enough to make the weapon useful for medium-range attacks. In a pinch, the shotgun can be used for sniping, though the spread of the pellets makes it hard to do much damage at long range.

Packs of weaker enemies are particularly vulnerable to shotgun fire, and it is often possible to kill two or more Zombiemen or Shotgun Guys with a single shot. It should usually kill an Imp with a well-aimed blast or a Demon in two, but this is often not the case. Against tougher enemies, such as Cacodemons , it is usually best to lunge forward and fire at short range, then dodge the enemy's attacks during the cocking sequence. This tactic works well when combined with circle strafing .

The shotgun is considered a light-medium weapon, stronger than the fists or pistols, so it is generally good for dealing with small groups of humanoids, and the occasional tough monster scattered in mazes.
For riot control, say large crowds of former humans, Imps, Demons, or several Hell Knights and Cacodemons, it is better to use available weapons with greater firepower such as the Plasma Gun and Rocket Launcher ; for Doom II the super shotgun is perhaps the best alternative since there is no splash damage and because it draws from the plentiful shell ammo pool.

The shotgun's main disadvantages are the slow rate of fire (which can leave the player vulnerable to counterattacks, especially in tight corridors), the pellet spread which weakens it at long range and the fact that the gun is difficult to use against tougher enemies such as a Baron of Hell for inexperienced players, especially in large numbers. However, these problems are less extreme than for the super shotgun. If shells are the only plentiful ammo, the shotgun is less wasteful and fires faster if one needs to snipe or deal with lone humanoids scattered in mazes.

The _Quake Engine_ introduced several features that would have simply been impossible on the _Doom Engine_ . Combined, these resulted in more interesting and varied level designs and gameplay. These features included;

### 3D

In contrast to _Doom’s_ 2\.5D set up, _Quake_ was fully 3D, with full mouse look, jumping and looking and aiming up and down. In addition, it featured fully polygonal enemies and world objects, and simple lighting and particle effects. 3D physics were also incorporated - grenades flew in a parabolic trajectory and bounced when they hit walls, ceilings and floors. This allowed for creative grenade use, such as bouncing them down shafts and around corners to hit unseen enemies from a safe position. Of course, the grenade launching ogres could do the same to you.
Gibs too would go flying in all directions, bounce along the floor and fall off walkways in a satisfyingly gory fashion.

_Quake’s_ level design took full advantage of the new engine’s capabilities. Enemies could appear above you on catwalks, but you could hide under said catwalks to avoid their fire.

Flying enemies, such as the floating _'Scrags'_ could hide above doorways and attack you from above and behind after you had passed through. _Quake_ demanded the player think three-dimensionally and encouraged using height to their advantage.

Some levels, in particular, the low gravity secret level _‘Ziggurat Vertigo’,_ took this verticality to the extreme, with a map that was taller than it was wide. Before first-person shooters became cinematic military campaigns, open-world sandboxes or esports arenas with weapon skins priced like small appliances, they were often cramped, loud, rude and wonderfully strange. In the middle of that strange period stood the Build engine, the technology behind Duke Nukem 3D and several other defining DOS shooters. It was not the cleanest engine, not the most technically pure, and not always the easiest to explain without making hand movements in the air. But it did something many engines never manage. It gave games a personality. Build was the work of Ken Silverman, a young programmer whose engine became the foundation for a whole branch of 90s FPS design.
Where Doom made abstract hellish arenas feel fast and readable, Build helped designers make cities that looked lived-in, even if everyone living there had apparently been abducted, mutated or replaced by pigs with shotguns.

Instead, Build used sectors, walls, sprites and clever rendering tricks to create places that felt more complex than they truly were.

This is where the engine’s character begins. Build was not trying to be a sterile simulator of reality. It was an efficient theatre machine. It gave level designers a box of stage tricks and said, more or less, make the player believe this city exists for the next ten minutes. In Duke Nukem 3D, that was enough. You did not need a fully accurate urban model. You needed a street, a cinema lobby, a rooftop, a bathroom mirror, a lift, some broken glass, a ridiculous alien and a vending machine that looked like it had seen things.

##### Why Duke Nukem 3D felt like a city, not a maze

Duke Nukem 3D is often remembered for its attitude, jokes and macho parody, but the game’s lasting power also comes from its spaces. Its levels were not just corridors with wallpaper. They had recognisable functions. A cinema looked like a cinema. A bar looked like a bar.

Build’s spaces were rarely elegant, but they were tactile. You could recognise what a room was supposed to be before the shooting started. Often, after the shooting stopped, it looked as if the room had made several poor life choices.

Duke Nukem 3D’s Los Angeles was not realistic in the modern sense. It was a compression of city clichés, action film sets and level-design necessities. Yet it felt fresh because it gave players context. You were not just in Episode 1, Level 2. You were in a cinema. You were not merely searching for a keycard. You were breaking into a location with a purpose. This small shift did a lot of work. It made levels memorable.

That was one of Build’s real gifts. It gave designers enough flexibility to create theme, joke and function in the same space. A room could be combat arena, punchline and navigational landmark. A bathroom could contain a mirror, a secret, a gag and an ambush. The result was a style of FPS design that rewarded nosiness.
In a Build game, curiosity was almost a weapon. Sometimes it was also how you found a hidden room full of explosives, which is the most 90s sentence available.

##### Not magic, just useful compromise

It is easy to overpraise old engines because nostalgia adds bloom lighting to everything. Build deserves admiration, but not mythology. It had limitations. Its handling of vertical space was clever rather than fully free. True room-over-room geometry was not its natural language. Designers had to understand its rules and work around its boundaries. Some effects were smoke and mirrors, though in fairness smoke and mirrors are also a perfectly valid design philosophy if the player is too busy fighting cultists to complain.

That compromise is exactly why Build is interesting. It was not powerful because it removed every constraint. It was powerful because its constraints were productive. They encouraged designers to build dense, legible, surprising spaces.

An engine is only as influential as the work it allows people to make with it. Build’s importance was not just in what it drew on screen, but in how it enabled level authors to think. Blood pushed the engine towards gothic horror, black comedy and nasty combat encounters. Other Build-powered games explored fantasy, science fiction, rural parody and licensed material with varying levels of success.

That variety shows how flexible the engine could be. It did not impose one exact mood.

Eternal is designed around mobility. Dashing, double-jumping, wall climbing, and meat hook traversal elevate level and combat design into almost platformer-like territory. **Difficulty and Progression**  
Doom Eternal is not forgiving, even on its default difficulty. Resource management and constant movement are mandatory. However, the game is fair—failure often feels like a failure to adapt or execute, not a flaw in design.

Battlemode is an asymmetric 2v1 PvP mode: two player-controlled demons versus one Doom Slayer.
While unique in concept, it didn’t quite gain a major foothold in the multiplayer shooter space.

The absence of traditional deathmatch (which was in Doom 2016) disappointed some fans, though mod support and invasions (added in later updates) offer additional longevity.

**Final Verdict: 9/10**  
Doom Eternal is a masterclass in modern FPS design—fast, intelligent, and gloriously violent. Its demand for precision and strategic aggression may overwhelm newcomers, but for players who embrace its rhythm, it offers some of the most rewarding combat in gaming.

It’s not without flaws—occasional platforming awkwardness, a divisive lore-heavy narrative, and a multiplayer mode that never quite took off—but none of these detract significantly from its status as one of the most finely-tuned shooters of the decade.
